Contactless Breathing-Rate Estimation from Video

This project estimates breathing rate from visible chest motion in ordinary video. It uses dense optical flow to turn frame-to-frame movement into a signal, then filters that signal and searches for the strongest repeating breathing rhythm.

View GitHub Repository
video → grayscale frames → chest motion → cumulative motion → band-pass filter → frequency spectrum → breaths/min → quality checks

1. Where the signal comes from

The pipeline measures two areas: the chest, where breathing motion should appear, and a background area that should stay still. The background gives us a reference for camera movement.

2. Raw optical-flow motion

Farneback optical flow estimates how pixels move between neighboring frames. We keep the vertical component and average it inside the chest region. The result is a frame-by-frame motion trace in pixels per frame.

3. From motion to a breathing wave

The frame-to-frame motion is a speed-like signal. A cumulative sum turns it into a position-like signal, then detrending and a band-pass filter remove drift and frequencies outside the allowed breathing range.

Key idea: optical flow gives “how much the chest moved since the last frame.” The cumulative sum reconstructs the overall rise-and-fall shape over time.

4. Frequency analysis

A periodogram asks: which repeating frequency explains this wave best? Frequency is measured in cycles per second (Hz), so the code multiplies by 60 to express the result as breaths per minute.

5. What failure cases look like

The quality checks do not just ask whether the code can output a number. They ask whether that number should be trusted.

6. Reference vs. estimated rate

The clean synthetic clips are recovered closely. The failure cases show why a rate estimate alone is not enough; quality flags matter.

9. Why the main design choices were made

Grayscale

The signal comes from movement, not color. Grayscale lowers computation while preserving the structure optical flow needs.

Lower resolution and frame rate

Breathing is slow, so full-resolution 30–60 FPS video is unnecessary for this experiment.

Vertical flow

The main visible breathing motion is chest rise and fall, so the vertical component is the most useful part of the motion field.

Band-pass filter

It removes very slow drift and fast noise, leaving the frequency range where a breathing rhythm is expected.

Background ROI

If the background moves almost as much as the chest, the camera is probably moving and the estimate should be questioned.

3×3 chest grid

Breathing should produce broadly consistent chest motion. Local fabric movement often breaks that agreement.

Limitations

This is an experimental computer-vision pipeline, not a medical device. The regions of interest and quality thresholds are manually defined, and the method still needs validation on a larger real-world dataset.

Built with Python, OpenCV, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Matplotlib, and SQLite.
